expectedText:
SINGLE-MEMBER LLC OPERATING AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Ventures, LLC

FORMATION AND MEMBERSHIP
Acme Ventures, LLC is a single-member limited liability company organized under the laws of Delaware. Jordan Lee is its sole member, holding a 100% membership interest.

FEDERAL TAX CLASSIFICATION
For federal tax purposes, Acme Ventures, LLC is, by default, disregarded as an entity separate from Jordan Lee — its income, deductions, and credits are reported on Jordan Lee's own tax return, rather than a separate company return, unless Acme Ventures, LLC affirmatively elects a different classification.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "unless the entity elects otherwise, a domestic eligible entity is— (i) A partnership if it has two or more members; or (ii) Disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, default federal tax classification of eligible entities (the 'check-the-box' rule) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  Known gap: This default applies automatically, with no election required — but it isn't the only option. A single-member LLC can elect to be taxed as a corporation, or potentially as an S corporation through a separate election, by filing the appropriate IRS form. This document doesn't say which classification is actually better for a given business — that depends on income level, self-employment tax exposure, and other facts specific to the business. Being disregarded for federal tax purposes has no effect on the LLC's separate legal existence under state law; those are two different questions, addressed by two different bodies of law. This is one federal regulation; no additional independent source was found restating this specific default classification separately.

HOW AND WHEN A DIFFERENT CLASSIFICATION GETS ELECTED
Changing away from the default disregarded-entity treatment isn't automatic — it takes filing IRS Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election). The effective date on that form has real limits: it can't be dated more than 75 days before the filing date, and can't be dated more than 12 months after it. Once Acme Ventures, LLC makes an election to change its classification, it generally can't elect a different classification again for 60 months from the effective date of that election, absent IRS permission.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "an eligible entity may elect to be classified other than as provided under paragraph (b) of this section, or to change its classification, by filing Form 8832, Entity Classification Election, with the service center designated on Form 8832."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(i) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, how an eligible entity elects its classification (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  "The effective date specified on Form 8832 can not be more than 75 days prior to the date on which the election is filed and can not be more than 12 months after the date on which the election is filed."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, the effective-date window for a classification election (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  "If an eligible entity makes an election under paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section to change its classification (other than an election made by an existing entity to change its classification as of the effective date of this section), the entity cannot change its classification by election again during the sixty months succeeding the effective date of the election."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iv) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, the sixty-month limitation on re-electing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current Treasury Regulations text. The 60-month lock-in has a narrow exception — the IRS may allow an earlier change if more than half the entity's ownership as of the later election is held by people who owned no interest at the time of the earlier one — but that relief isn't automatic, and this document doesn't state the full standard for obtaining it. This document doesn't cover the separate, S-corporation-specific election under 26 U.S.C. § 1362, which has its own timing rule.

LIMITED LIABILITY
Acme Ventures, LLC's debts and liabilities are its own — they don't become Jordan Lee's personal debts or liabilities solely because Jordan Lee is its member.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability shield (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  "A member of a limited liability company shall be subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and shall also be personally liable under a judgment of a court or for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company, whether that liability or obligation arises in contract, tort, or otherwise, under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for any debt, obligation, or liability of the corporation; except that the failure to hold meetings of members or managers or the failure to observe formalities pertaining to the calling or conduct of meetings shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that a member or the members have alter ego or personal liability for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company where the articles of organization or operating agreement do not expressly require the holding of meetings of members or managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, alter ego liability and the meeting-formalities carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used here as real evidence that a liability shield with a specific, real exception is a genuine feature of LLC law generally — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company. The shield isn't absolute: a member can still be held personally liable under the common-law 'alter ego' doctrine, the same doctrine that can pierce a corporation's liability shield, under the same or similar circumstances. One thing that specifically does not count against a member on its own, at least under this statute: failing to hold formal member or manager meetings doesn't establish alter ego liability by itself, as long as the articles of organization or the operating agreement itself doesn't require holding them.

RECORDS AND TAX RETURN ACCESS
A member — or someone a member's interest in Acme Ventures, LLC has been transferred to — has the right, for purposes reasonably related to their interest, to inspect and copy Acme Ventures, LLC's required records during normal business hours, and to obtain a written copy of Acme Ventures, LLC's federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year, promptly after they become available.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Each member, manager, and transferee has the right, upon reasonable request, for purposes reasonably related to the interest of that person as a member, manager, or transferee, to each of the following: (1) To inspect and copy during normal business hours any of the records required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (2) To obtain in writing from the limited liability company, promptly after becoming available, a copy of the limited liability company’s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, member and transferee inspection and tax-return rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.10.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This right belongs to a transferee (someone who receives an economic interest, such as an heir, without becoming a full member) as well as to members themselves — it isn't limited to people with voting rights. This document doesn't restate the additional annual and interim financial-reporting duties this same statute imposes once an LLC has more than 35 members.

INITIAL CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION
Jordan Lee has contributed the following to Acme Ventures, LLC as an initial capital contribution:

Cash: $_______________
Other property (describe): _______________________________________________

MANAGEMENT
Acme Ventures, LLC is managed by Jordan Lee as its sole member. Jordan Lee has full authority to make all decisions on behalf of Acme Ventures, LLC, including entering contracts, opening and operating bank accounts, and conducting business in the company's name.

DISTRIBUTIONS
Acme Ventures, LLC may distribute available cash or property to Jordan Lee at the times and in the amounts Jordan Lee determines.

DISSOLUTION
Acme Ventures, LLC will continue until dissolved by Jordan Lee or as otherwise required by law. Upon dissolution, Acme Ventures, LLC's debts and liabilities will be paid or provided for first, with any remaining assets distributed to Jordan Lee.

WHAT HAPPENS ON THE SOLE MEMBER'S DEATH
A single-member LLC does not automatically dissolve the moment its sole member dies. State law's default dissolution trigger for a membership gap is 90 consecutive days with no members — but on the death of a sole member, that member's interest can pass directly to their heirs, successors, or assigns by will or other applicable law, and that heir or successor becomes a substituted member without needing anyone's permission or consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the limited liability company has no members, except that, on the death of a natural person who is the sole member of a limited liability company, the status of the member, including a membership interest, may pass to one or more heirs, successors, and assigns of the member by will or applicable law. An heir, successor, or assign of the member’s interest becomes a substituted member pursuant to paragraph (4) of subdivision (c) of Section 17704.01, subject to administration as provided by applicable law, without the permission or consent of the heirs, successors, or assigns or those administering the estate of the deceased member."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, sole member's death and heir succession (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.01.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default succession rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This default rule doesn't override estate administration itself — the interest still passes subject to whatever probate or other administration process otherwise applies to the deceased member's estate. This document doesn't say who the heir, successor, or assign actually is for a given member; that's a matter of the member's own estate plan (or intestacy law if there isn't one), not something this operating agreement can settle on its own.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Adopted and agreed to by the sole member:

Member: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
